abstract: Illegal killing for ivory is the primary threat to the endangered African savanna elephant (Loxodonta africana). Botswana has the world's largest elephant population and experienced little poaching during the continent-wide poaching outbreak of the early 2000's. In 2018, however, evidence of widespread elephant poaching in Botswana began to appear, with an estimated 385 elephants poached. Here, we update the status of elephant poaching in northern Botswana with new data collected in 2023-2026. We also used spatial models to determine the factors associated with elephant poaching locations and to better understand poacher behavior. From late 2023 through mid-2026, we located 202 poached elephants in a ~10,000 km2 area of northern Botswana, north and east of the Okavango Delta and mostly west of Chobe National Park. All poached elephants were believed to be adult males. Using point process models, we found that, depending on the method used to locate carcasses, poaching locations were associated with greater distance from roads, higher slope, lower distance to military posts, higher Enhanced Vegetation Index in the dry season, and greater distance from the Namibia border than random points. The poaching outbreak documented in 2018 was not transient: illegal killing for ivory appears to have continued. Because poachers are targeting adult males, their numbers could become depleted in our study area, which has implications for elephant social behavior, legal elephant hunting, and ecotourism. We encourage the government of Botswana to take immediate action against poaching, including improving monitoring and strengthening transboundary cooperation.
